title: Round Hill is suing Suno and Anthropic for up to $1B apiece. It isn’t looking to settle.

reading.body:
Suno and Udio are AI music generators trained on copyrighted songs scraped without permission from the internet, including YouTube, Deezer, and Genius. The companies did not disclose which music was used for training. Record labels demonstrated that the systems could reproduce sections of famous copyrighted songs when given specific prompts, generating output that closely replicated works by artists including The Beatles, Frank Sinatra, Michael Jackson, and Mariah Carey.

This is a model trained on data obtained without authorization and deployed to generate content that reproduces copyrighted material. The failure occurred at training time, when the companies collected thousands of protected works without permission or disclosure, and continued in deployment, when the systems produced outputs that infringed existing copyrights. Catching this would have required either obtaining licenses for the training data or implementing filtering to prevent the system from generating content that matched copyrighted works.

Multiple lawsuits were filed by record labels, individual artists, and music publishers. A German court ruled against Suno in a copyright case brought by GEMA. Some record labels reached settlements with the companies, though it is not established whether these represent findings of liability or business arrangements.

summary:
Major record labels including Universal Music Group, Sony Music, Warner Music, Capitol Records, and Atlantic Records have filed separate lawsuits against Udio and Suno, two popular AI music generators. The labels accuse both companies of scraping thousands of copyrighted songs without permission to train their AI models and then directly reproducing sections of famous songs in their generated music. The lawsuits claim the companies have been deliberately secretive about their training data and that neither company will disclose which music was used.

To support their case, the record labels demonstrated their ability to recreate versions of well-known copyrighted songs by using specific prompts in both AI generators. They submitted a list of thousands of copyrighted works they claim were scraped, including music from artists like The Beatles, Frank Sinatra, Michael Jackson, and many others. Examples in the lawsuits show AI-generated songs that closely replicate famous tracks, including one that nearly duplicates Mariah Carey's "All I Want for Christmas Is You." The cases represent a major legal battle over how generative AI services should handle copyrighted material.
